messages.author: fb5901bc16a12a35
messages.subject: Spatial Replication and Abundance Predictions
parts:
Hi all,

Frequent reader, first time poster here.

Hopefully this will be a quick and easy question to answer, however I have been unable to find an answer through related papers or searching this group. 

I am estimating abundance of a fish, using the unmarked function pcount(). My study design was as follows: Within each of 2 streams I sampled several 120m stream reaches (the site level), and then 12 independent 10m^2 plots within each reach (the observational level). I am using these plots as spatial replicates in place of temporal replicates typically used in these models. Essentially, instead of re-sampling X number of times I sampled 12 plots within the same site as my replicates. So I have a count associated with each replicate of each site. 

I modeled with my covariates for detection and abundance and came up with my fitted models. Using either predict() or ranef() I get a matrix which includes a column related to my predictions. For example ranef produces:

 Mean                   Mode 2.5% 97.5%
 [1,]  5.35481832    5    3     8
 [2,] 22.13031890   22   17    28
 [3,] 25.37614331   26   20    29
 [4,]  3.53496729    3    1     6
 [5,]  0.00203653    0    0     0
 [6,]  9.15349140    9    6    12
 [7,] 15.54310502   15   12    20
 [8,] 15.85494164   16   12    21
 [9,]  7.79657345    7    5    12
[10,]  5.92160048    6    3     9

I would interpret the Mean column here as representing the predicted abundance for a site when using the typical temporal replication template.

My question is: Would I be correct in interpreting these results in that the Mean column represents the predicted abundance for the area corresponding to one plot (or replicate), not the combination of all 12 plot areas (total area sampled in a site) given the spatial replication template. So with a plot area of 10m^2 the site listed as 1 would have an average predicted density of 0.53 fish/m^2 not 0.046 fish/m^2 if it is a prediction for the total area sampled (120m^2).

I do have R code for all of the modeling process, but I am hopeful that this brief description of my study design will be sufficient to answer the question.

Thanks,

Davy Black

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Spatial Replication and Abundance Predictions
parts:
Hi Davy,

Yep, these are site-specific values and not summaries across the entire set of sites (although those summaries could be derived).

For a more thorough treatment, you might look at some of the references associated with ranef-methods in the package's reference manual, but: informally, values returned by ranef might be thought of as estimates of the state variable (abundance, occupancy, etc.) at that particular site/time. The predict function returns predictions.

Cheers,

John

messages.subject: Re: Spatial Replication and Abundance Predictions
parts:
Thanks for the speedy reply John,

I will take a further look into ranef, I hadn't really thought of it that way because in my case the returned values from ranef and predict are ultimately quite similar. Ranef does return slightly smaller confidence intervals, but I take it that is because of the stricter association with the observed values in its computational approach than predict.

Thanks again,

Davy

I think it is problematic to use the 'plots as spatial replicates in place of temporal replicates'. This would require the assumption that abundance is exactly the same at each plot within a stream. 

Richard

parts:
Richard,

I guess I was mistaken, I had thought that as long as the state parameter was modeled with covariates, and not held constant then the covariates were used to match changes in the state parameter to measured covariates at the replications. If all plots had equal potential to hold the same number of individuals, and covariates hypothesized to hold potential to explain variation in abundance across those plots were used to account for any variation that was seen, is that not the purpose of including observational covariates? 

Or should I be looking into an open population model such as pcountOpen perhaps?

Any further direction from yourself or other readers would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,

Davy

messages.author: 403be63af7ebf220
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Spatial Replication and Abundance Predictions
parts:
Hi Davy,

The observation covariates are meant to account for variation in detection probability conditional on site-specific abundance. You cannot model variation in abundance as a function of observation covariates because abundance is assumed to be constant among replicate surveys. Without replicates at your plots, I don't see how you could reliably estimate abundance and detection probability. 

Richard
